mappings.note: argues from one cell component to why a rooted plant survives wind and rain, so the organism-level role (LO-3); the plant-versus-animal framing of the stem carries LO-1. Not LO-2, which would only describe the wall.
predicts from a single structural property of the wall (rigidity) what the cell loses; no plant/animal contrast is demanded and no tonicity is named, so LO-2 rather than LO-1 or LO-5.
asks why the pieces must be equal and pre-weighed, i.e. controlled variables and a baseline; the osmosis concept is assumed, so the experiment-design outcome, not C-3.1-LO-5.
answered by knowing leucoplasts are pigment-free plastids; a feature of a plastid type, not an organism-level role (LO-3).

the task is to produce a graphical model of the cell from shape clues, which is the C8.1 competency (geometric/graphical models); C-8.1-LO-1 is excluded because it requires a low-cost material model, not a drawing. LO-2 covers the organelle features represented.
form-function reasoning about organelle shape and surface-area-to-volume; it never asks what respiration does, so LO-2 not LO-4.
turns on mitosis giving identical diploid cells versus meiosis giving varied haploid ones; exactly the similarity/variation role of the two divisions.
three organelle-versus-organelle contrasts (membrane/wall, RER/SER, chloroplast/chromoplast); LO-1 is reserved for plant-versus-animal and prokaryote-versus-eukaryote contrasts.
the distractors assert salt moved into the cell, so the marked discrimination is water movement versus solute movement, i.e. osmosis against diffusion, rather than naming the tonicity.
identification of labelled parts on a cell diagram plus their stated jobs; recall of organelle features, not a traced pathway (LO-4).
the whole item is a present-in-plant / absent-in-animal sort; nothing else is tested.
resolved by knowing leucoplasts are non-photosynthetic plastids; a plastid-type feature, not a claim about roots as an organ (LO-3).
explicitly asks 'structurally and functionally' for two organelles; the shared-DNA point is incidental here, so LO-2 rather than the biomolecule outcome C-4.2-LO-1.
the key is where the genetic biomolecule sits (nucleus and mitochondria), not what those organelles do; the biomolecule strand, not organelle function (LO-2).
two of the three parts ask for the hypothesis under test and an improvement to the design; the osmosis explanation is only the third part.
a present/absent table across bacterial and animal cells; the prokaryote-eukaryote half of LO-1.
'Why is Cup A necessary' is control design (C-8.2-LO-1); the boiled-potato cup is what demonstrates that osmosis needs a living semi-permeable boundary (C-3.1-LO-5).
the error to spot is that SER does not make cellulose, i.e. a wrong organelle-function pairing; recall of stated functions, so LO-2 rather than LO-4's traced activities.
predicts what stops when an in-cell activity (respiration and ATP supply) ends; about the activity, not the organelle's description.
contact inhibition is the brake on mitosis, so the cell-division outcome is the nearest fit; the frame names no outcome for growth regulation or cancer.
traces a multi-organelle route ER to Golgi to vesicle to membrane (LO-4); the stem's premise, that the membrane is protein plus lipid, is the biomolecule strand.
the consequence is chromosome doubling each generation, i.e. why meiosis halves the number; the role of the two divisions.
osmotic dehydration of spoilage microbes is the science (LO-5), set inside a livelihood case with a waste-and-income angle, which is what C-5.2-LO-1 asks for.
the options set bacteria against algae, fungi and protozoa, so the choice is kingdom-level cellular diversity (C4.1) resting on the prokaryote/eukaryote line (LO-1).
the 0.1 mm figure exists only to justify using a microscope to see cells; the frame has no instrument-theory outcome, so the slide-observation outcome is the closest available. Weak fit.
